steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on predicting Alzheimer's disease progression from MRI using cross-domain self-supervised learning. Cover the annotation problem in medical imaging, transfer learning and SSL, prior work on AD progression prediction, and end with our approach and main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Labeled data is scarce in medical imaging; transfer learning from natural images
- Self-supervised learning and its limited use in medical imaging
- Task: predicting Alzheimer's disease progression from MRI
- Prior work on AD progression and why progress is slow
- Our cross-domain SSL approach and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Labeled data scarce
  - reliable AI needs efficient DL + large annotated data
  - labeling medical images slow, expensive; complex annotation, high expertise
  - transfer learning from natural images increasingly popular (cite)
  - fine-tuning from supervised or self-supervised ImageNet models effective (cite) but not always, domain mismatch (cite)
- SSL
  - great success in CV downstream tasks where labels expensive (cite)
  - medicine well-poised: huge amounts of images from hospital and non-hospital settings
  - but limited attention; few studies: classification (cite), segmentation (cite)
- Our task
  - self-supervised DL model predicting AD progression from high dimensional MRI
  - AD: slowly progressing, degeneration of brain cells; symptoms years after onset
  - early prognosis + treatment critical, non-reversible fatal damage; earlier treatment, personalized care
- Prior work
  - coarse categories (MCI, dementia), conversion e.g. MCI to dementia (cite)
  - clinical trials need finer scale, narrow populations (only MCI)
  - alternative: predict cognitive/functional test outcomes, continuous values -> regression, more granular
  - RNN, CNN approaches on MRI
  - one work: MinimalRNN, longitudinal clinical info + cross-sectional tabular imaging features (cite)
  - another: ensemble of stacked CNN + BiLSTM, time series clinical + derived imaging features (cite)
  - CNN on raw imaging; multi-task interaction layers, feature decoupling + feature interaction modules (cite)
  - little progress: hard design requirements, no large homogeneous early-AD datasets, noisy endpoints
  - image-derived features to handle raw MRI variability, small datasets
  - single dataset (cohort) -> poor generalizability; few annotated images -> domain shift, heterogeneity
- Our approach
  - cross-domain self-supervised transfer learning, transferable generalizable representations
  - SSL on unlabeled large-scale natural images + in-domain medical dataset from 11 internal and external studies
  - fine-tune for disease progression with limited labels
  - compare supervised / self-supervised models pretrained on natural, medical, or both
  - findings (1) SSL natural then SSL medical best, less reliance on annotation (2) SSL on medical beats SSL on natural for regression

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Building reliable and robust artificial intelligence systems needs efficient deep learning techniques, and also large volumes of data that have to be collected and annotated for training. But making a labeled dataset often takes a lot of time and money, for example in medical imaging, because the annotation tasks are complex and manual interpretation needs high expertise. Transfer learning from natural images is becoming more and more popular as a way to deal with the lack of annotations in medical imaging. Many experimental studies show that fine-tuning from supervised or self-supervised ImageNet models is effective, but it does not always improve performance because of the domain mismatch problem.

At the same time, self-supervised learning (SSL) has been very successful in many downstream computer vision applications where labeling is expensive and takes a long time. Medical research and healthcare should benefit a lot from SSL approaches, since hospitals and non-hospital settings generate unprecedented amounts of medical images. Even so, SSL in the medical image domain has not received much attention. Only a few studies have looked at the impact of SSL in medical image analysis, and only for limited applications like classification and segmentation.

In this study we develop a self-supervised deep learning model to predict the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from high dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). AD is a disease that progresses slowly and is caused by degeneration of brain cells, and patients show clinical symptoms years after the disease starts. So an accurate prognosis and treatment of AD in its early stage is critical to prevent brain damage that is non-reversible and fatal. If AD progression can be predicted accurately, clinicians can start treatment earlier and give more personalized care.

- Prior work on AD progression
  - many methods classify into coarse categories (MCI, dementia) or predict conversion, e.g. MCI to dementia
  - clinical trials need a finer scale, populations narrowly defined (only MCI)
  - alternative: regress outcomes of cognitive and functional tests, continuous values, more granular
  - RNN/CNN methods: MinimalRNN with longitudinal clinical info + tabular imaging features; stacked CNN + BiLSTM ensemble; CNN on raw imaging with multi-task interaction layers
- Why progress is slow
  - difficult design requirements; no large homogeneous datasets with early stage AD; noisy endpoints
  - image-derived features; single cohort training, few annotated images -> domain shift, heterogeneity
- Our approach
  - cross-domain SSL: natural images + in-domain dataset from 11 internal and external studies; fine-tune with limited labels
  - findings (1) and (2)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Building reliable and robust artificial intelligence systems needs efficient deep learning techniques, and also large volumes of data that have to be collected and annotated for training. But making a labeled dataset often takes a lot of time and money, for example in medical imaging, because the annotation tasks are complex and manual interpretation needs high expertise. Transfer learning from natural images is becoming more and more popular as a way to deal with the lack of annotations in medical imaging. Many experimental studies show that fine-tuning from supervised or self-supervised ImageNet models is effective, but it does not always improve performance because of the domain mismatch problem.

At the same time, self-supervised learning (SSL) has been very successful in many downstream computer vision applications where labeling is expensive and takes a long time. Medical research and healthcare should benefit a lot from SSL approaches, since hospitals and non-hospital settings generate unprecedented amounts of medical images. Even so, SSL in the medical image domain has not received much attention. Only a few studies have looked at the impact of SSL in medical image analysis, and only for limited applications like classification and segmentation.

In this study we develop a self-supervised deep learning model to predict the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from high dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). AD is a disease that progresses slowly and is caused by degeneration of brain cells, and patients show clinical symptoms years after the disease starts. So an accurate prognosis and treatment of AD in its early stage is critical to prevent brain damage that is non-reversible and fatal. If AD progression can be predicted accurately, clinicians can start treatment earlier and give more personalized care.

Many existing methods for predicting AD progression classify patients into coarse categories like Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) or dementia, or predict conversion from one category to another (e.g. MCI to dementia). But clinical trials need a more fine-grained scale, since trial populations are usually narrowly defined (e.g. only MCI). Another approach is to predict the outcome of cognitive and functional tests, which are continuous numerical values. If the prediction is framed as regression and not classification, prognostic models can give more granular estimates of disease progression. Recently a few deep learning approaches, including recurrent neural networks (RNN) and convolutional neural networks (CNN), have been proposed to predict disease progression of AD patients from MRIs. One work adapted MinimalRNN to combine longitudinal clinical information with cross-sectional tabular imaging features to regress endpoints. Another work used an ensemble model based on stacked CNN and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) to predict the endpoints from the fusion of time series clinical features and derived imaging features. Recently, some methods have started to use CNN based models to extract features from raw medical images. A third work applied a CNN with multi-task interaction layers made of feature decoupling modules and a feature interaction module to predict disease progression.

Even though there is demand, there has not been much progress, because the design requirements are difficult, there are no large-scale homogeneous datasets with early stage AD patients, and the endpoints are noisy and can be hard to predict. A lot of prior work used image-derived features to get around the complexity and high variability of raw MRIs and the small datasets. Most current prognosis models are trained on one dataset (i.e. cohort), and this limits how well they generalize to other cohorts. They also use a limited number of annotated images, which can cause problems like domain shift and heterogeneity.

We built a cross-domain self-supervised transfer learning approach that learns transferable and generalizable representations for medical images. Our approach uses SSL both on unlabeled large-scale natural images and on an in-domain medical image dataset put together from 11 different internal and external studies. These representations can then be fine-tuned for downstream tasks like disease progression prediction using limited labeled data from the clinical setting. We evaluated different supervised and self-supervised models pretrained on natural images, medical images, or both. Our experiments show that (1) self-supervised pretraining on natural images followed by self-supervised learning on unlabeled medical images is better than the other transfer learning methods, which shows that SSL can reduce the reliance on data annotation compared to supervised approaches, and (2) self-supervised models pretrained on medical images are better than those pretrained on natural images, meaning that SSL on medical images gives discriminative feature representations for the regression task.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Developing reliable and robust artificial intelligence systems requires efficient deep learning techniques as well as the creation and annotation of large volumes of training data. However, constructing a labeled dataset is often time-consuming and expensive, for example in the medical imaging domain, due to the complexity of annotation tasks and the high expertise required for manual interpretation. To alleviate the lack of annotations in medical imaging, transfer learning from natural images is becoming increasingly popular [1,2,3,4]. Although numerous experimental studies indicate that fine-tuning from either supervised or self-supervised ImageNet models is effective ([5,6,7,8,9,10]), it does not always improve performance because of the domain mismatch problem [11].

Meanwhile, self-supervised learning (SSL) has shown great success in many downstream computer vision applications where labeling is expensive and time-consuming [12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20]. Medical research and healthcare are especially well-placed to benefit from SSL approaches, given the unprecedented amounts of medical images generated in hospital and non-hospital settings. Despite this, SSL in the medical image domain has received limited attention, and only a few studies have investigated its impact in medical image analysis, for limited applications including classification [21,22,23,24,25,26] and segmentation [27,28,29,30].

In this study, we focus on developing a self-supervised deep learning model for predicting the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from high dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). AD is a slowly progressing disease caused by the degeneration of brain cells, and patients show clinical symptoms years after its onset. Accurate prognosis and treatment of AD in its early stage is therefore critical to prevent non-reversible and fatal brain damage. By accurately predicting AD progression, clinicians can start treatment earlier and provide more personalized care.

Many existing methods for predicting AD progression classify patients into coarse categories, such as Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) or dementia, or predict conversion from one category to another (e.g. MCI to dementia) [31,32,33]. However, clinical trials require a more fine-grained measurement scale, since trial populations are typically narrowly defined (e.g. only MCI). An alternative is to predict the outcome of cognitive and functional tests, which are continuous numerical values. By framing the prediction as a regression rather than a classification, prognostic models can offer more granular estimates of disease progression. Recently, a few deep learning approaches, including recurrent neural networks (RNN) and convolutional neural networks (CNN), have been proposed for predicting disease progression of AD patients from MRIs. [34] adapted MinimalRNN to integrate longitudinal clinical information and cross-sectional tabular imaging features for regressing endpoints. [35] used an ensemble model based on stacked CNN and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) to predict the endpoints from the fusion of time series clinical features and derived imaging features. More recently, several methods have started to employ CNN based models to extract features from raw medical images. [36] applied a CNN with multi-task interaction layers composed of feature decoupling modules and a feature interaction module to predict disease progression.

Despite the demand, little progress has been made, because of difficult design requirements, the lack of large-scale, homogeneous datasets containing early stage AD patients, and noisy endpoints that can be hard to predict. Much prior work has relied on image-derived features to overcome the complexity and high variability of raw MRIs and the small datasets. Most current prognosis models are trained on a single dataset (i.e. cohort), which limits their generalizability to other cohorts, and they use a limited number of annotated images, which can lead to problems such as domain shift and heterogeneity.

We established a cross-domain self-supervised transfer learning approach that learns transferable and generalizable representations for medical images. Our approach applies SSL to both unlabeled large-scale natural images and an in-domain medical image dataset compiled from 11 different internal and external studies. These representations can then be fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as disease progression prediction using limited labeled data from the clinical setting. We evaluated different supervised and self-supervised models pretrained on natural images, medical images, or both. Our extensive experiments show that (1) self-supervised pretraining on natural images followed by self-supervised learning on unlabeled medical images outperforms alternative transfer learning methods, indicating that SSL can reduce the reliance on data annotation compared to supervised approaches, and (2) self-supervised models pretrained on medical images outperform those pretrained on natural images, suggesting that SSL on medical images yields discriminative feature representations for the regression task.

References:
